title: Identifiability in Quantum State, Process, and Network Tomography
authors: Athira Kalavampara Raghunadhan, Matheus Guedes De Andrade, Don Towsley, Indrakshi Dey, Daniel Kilper, Nicola Marchetti
abstract: Quantum State Tomography (QST), Quantum Process Tomography (QPT), and Quantum Network Tomography (QNT) are related parameter-estimation problems that aim to reconstruct different physical quantities. QST estimates an unknown quantum state, represented by its density matrix, from the measurement outcomes. QPT characterises an unknown quantum channel using known input states and measurements of the corresponding outputs. QNT, in contrast, aims to infer parameters associated with individual links from end-to-end probe measurements collected at accessible monitor nodes. A key distinction among the three tomography problems lies in the conditions required to achieve identifiability, the ability to determine unknown parameters uniquely from the available measurement statistics. In QST and QPT, the experimenter can choose an Informationally Complete (IC) measurement set. QNT limits the reachable measurements to what topology and monitor placement allow, so the admissible probe paths fix the information available about the link parameters. This work studies all three tomography problems through a common Fisher Information Matrix (FIM). We factorise QNT FIM and show that its rank equals the rank of the path-link incidence matrix at every interior parameter value, so local and global identifiability coincide. We then show that QST and QPT attain full rank under IC settings, QNT loses rank when the probe paths leave link parameters indistinguishable, and increasing the number of copies scales the FIM eigenvalues while leaving its rank fixed.
summary: This work compares the mathematical requirements for determining unknown parameters in Quantum State, Process, and Network Tomography. Using the Fisher Information Matrix, the authors show that while state and process tomography are robust under ideal measurements, network tomography is highly sensitive to the physical topology and the paths chosen for probing the links. This highlights the structural constraints inherent in distributed quantum measurements.
main_problem: The paper compares the conditions required for parameter identifiability across three quantum tomography tasks: State (QST), Process (QPT), and Network (QNT).
main_result: While QST and QPT achieve full rank under Informationally Complete measurements, QNT's identifiability critically depends on the topology and placement of probe paths relative to the underlying network links.
method: Identifiability is rigorously assessed by analyzing the rank of the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) for each tomography problem.
model_or_system: The study models quantum systems using density matrices ($ho$) for state estimation, quantum channels ($\mathcal{E}$) for process characterization, and a quantum network structured as an undirected graph $G=(V, E)$ for link parameter inference.
key_observables: The rank of the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) determines identifiability; specific observables include measurement probabilities $p_m$ and link parameters $\mathbf{w}$.
important_parameters: The number of independent measurement copies ($N$) scales the FIM eigenvalues linearly but does not change the rank if the measurement set is insufficient.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the FIM expressions are derived for one copy per measurement configuration, and QNT requires probe paths to provide independent information about the links.
figures_summary: Figure 2 illustrates that for insufficient probe paths, the FIM remains singular (zero eigenvalue persists across $N$), whereas sufficient probes lead to all eigenvalues growing linearly with $N$.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the three tomography problems, develops the FIM formalism for each, analyzes the rank conditions for QST and QPT (showing IC sufficiency), and then focuses on the structural constraints imposed by the graph topology for QNT.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous mathematical framework (FIM analysis) to determine when quantum parameters (states, channels, or network links) can be uniquely determined from experimental measurements, which is crucial for designing practical quantum experiments.
